name: seq_read
purpose: Page-hit upper bound for a single stream, and a stress test for bank-group ordering.
description: 8000 AR (read) transactions on one core, one AXI id (0), 64 bytes each, strictly sequential addresses starting at 0x10000000 (addr_i = base + i*64).

With this config's address mapping (row bits [11:26], bankgroup bits [27:28], bank bits [29:30]), a sequential stream stays in the same row for 2048/64 = 32 accesses before a row conflict, and only rotates bankgroup once every 2^16 rows -- i.e. essentially never over 8000 transactions. So this workload should show a high page-hit rate (row reuse works) but ALSO a near-100% bankgroup_reuse_rate_pct (every column command pays tCCD_L, not tCCD_S), because bankgroup is not the fastest-changing field in this mapping. That combination -- high hit rate, capped bandwidth -- is the point: it isolates the bank-group-ordering pathology described in README.md 'Bank-group ordering' from row-buffer behavior, which alone would predict much higher bandwidth than actually comes out.
numbers_in_prose: Numbers quoted in description/sanity_checks are from the run at authoring time and are NOT kept in sync with the model; they explain the reasoning, not the current values. golden.json holds the current numbers. The reasoning is what should be re-checked when a value moves -- if it no longer holds, that is a finding.
rng: none -- pure arithmetic sequence, no randomness
observed_metrics: see golden.json in this directory -- it is the authoritative snapshot, regenerated with --update-golden whenever model behavior deliberately changes. Numbers were duplicated here once and silently went stale the first time the timing model was fixed.
sanity_checks: sequential workload shows LOW row-conflict rate (3.1%, from the expected 1-in-32 row rollover) -- OK, matches the address-mapping arithmetic above
